clue.text: Former party leader could hear furry animal move slowly

indicators.note: one could hear the phrase spoken and catch a politician's name in it, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: a mink is a furry animal and to amble is to move slowly: MINK AMBLE

explanation.surface: Someone claims to hear a furry creature creeping about.
explanation.walkthrough: Say MINK AMBLE quickly and it runs into the name of Menzies (Ming) Campbell, who led the Liberal Democrats from 2006 to 2007.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Menzies Campbell, known as Ming, was leader of the UK Liberal Democrats, so a former head of a political party.

clue.text: One's sole of foot might get stuck in gum?

parts.note: one is = I am, shortened to I'M
planta is the Latin for the sole, and plant is an old word for the sole of the foot

explanation.surface: Something on the bottom of a shoe gets stuck in chewing gum.
explanation.walkthrough: The gum is not chewing gum but the gum of the mouth, where a dental fixture is screwed in.
explanation.definitionFit: A dental fitting is fixed into the jawbone beneath the gum, so it is literally lodged there.

clue.text: Too much of it when eating may leave stomach very upset internally!

definitions.text: Too much of it when eating

indicators.note: the inner letters are thrown about while the outer ones stay put, so this signals a rearrangement

parts.note: gut is another word for the stomach
so means very, as in 'so good'

explanation.surface: A warning that greedy eating ends in indigestion.
explanation.walkthrough: GUT + SO gives GUTSO; 'upset internally' shuffles only the middle, UTS becoming UST. 'may leave' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Relish or zest; eating with too much enthusiasm is what causes the upset stomach.

clue.text: A funky ploy by Shakespeare?

parts.note: a botched scheme is a farce of mistakes, which is also the title of one of the Bard's early plays

explanation.surface: Someone describes a strange scheme devised by the Bard.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'funky' (bungled, cowardly) ploy is a series of blunders; the question mark points to the play about two sets of mistaken twins.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of a Shakespeare farce also describes a chaotic plan undone by mistakes.

clue.text: Investigators overheard how government might make a killing

definitions.text: how government might make a killing

indicators.note: what is overheard is sound only, so a word spoken that matches another spelt differently

parts.note: private eyes are private detectives

explanation.surface: Detectives listening in on a government plotting murder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make a killing' means make a lot of money, by selling off state industries, not murder.
explanation.definitionFit: Selling state-owned industries to private buyers can earn a government a large one-off profit.

clue.text: Gradually remove media boss and get taken on by elite university

parts.note: ED is short for editor, the boss of a newspaper

indicators.note: the word get takes the university on board, so it holds it inside

parts.note: OU can stand for Oxford University

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor and his son are admitted to Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken on by' signals a container: the verb takes the university inside it. OU for Oxford University is a crossword convention, though the Open University often uses the same letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To push someone out little by little, as a rival slowly displaced from a position.

clue.text: What's found in shirt, not head? Either, in fact!

definitions.text: What's found in shirt, not head? Either, in fact!

indicators.note: the first letter of the word is dropped, its head cut off

parts.note: a blouse is a woman's shirt

explanation.surface: A riddle about something found in a shirt but not on the head.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay drops the first letter of BLOUSE, and the whole clue defines: this parasite lives in clothing and in hair, hence 'Either, in fact!'
explanation.definitionFit: A small parasitic insect infests both clothes (body lice) and the scalp (head lice).

clue.text: Clear ice off root

indicators.note: food that has gone off is spoilt, so the letters are spoilt into a new order

explanation.surface: Instructions to de-ice a plant root.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a root vegetable, a knobbly variety of celery grown for its swollen base.

clue.text: Passed water ebbing near high water mark?

indicators.note: an ebbing tide flows back, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: to pass water is to urinate, peed

explanation.surface: Someone urinating as the tide goes out by the shoreline.
explanation.walkthrough: On a sounding line the unmarked fathoms between the marks are called deeps, so this sits near a water mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors' lead lines have 'marks' and, between them, unmarked 'deeps' measuring water depth.

clue.text: Vital evidence of two possible causes of death …

parts.note: tobacco use is a cause of death
a firearm is another cause of death

explanation.surface: A coroner's report listing ways someone might have died.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase for incontrovertible proof of guilt, like a still-warm weapon at a crime scene.

clue.text: … not to mention a cause of death excluding heroin

indicators.note: the drug's letter is left out of the phrase

parts.note: something deadly is a lethal one
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A report on a death that rules out drug overdose.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom meaning 'much less' or 'still less', used to add something even more unlikely.

clue.text: Water bird at either side of rocky cove

indicators.note: the two letters of at are placed on both sides, enclosing the rest
something rocky is unsteady, so the letters wobble into a new order

explanation.surface: A bird seen on the edges of a craggy inlet.
explanation.walkthrough: VOCE, from cove, sits between A and T.
explanation.definitionFit: A black-and-white wading bird with an upcurved bill, emblem of the RSPB.

clue.text: Stuart's autobiography perhaps delivered in instalments

definitions.meaning: Stuart Little, the mouse of children's fiction
done gradually, a bit at a time

explanation.walkthrough: Stuart Little is the mouse hero of E B White's children's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means gradually, and a memoir by a character surnamed Little would be by Little.

clue.text: What might be grated in end of cheese 'n' ham melt

definitions.text: What might be grated in end of cheese 'n' ham melt

indicators.note: the last letter of the word is taken
grated cheese is shredded, so the letters are shredded into a new order

explanation.surface: Making a cheese and ham toastie with grated topping.
explanation.walkthrough: E (end of cheese) and NHAMMELT are mixed; the whole clue also describes the cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: A Swiss cheese with holes, often grated over a toasted sandwich.

clue.text: Postholder and temp might be told to stuff it?

definitions.meaning: something that holds the post, a letter cover

definitions.text: temp might be told to stuff it?
definitions.meaning: a temporary office worker is often given the task of filling mailers

explanation.walkthrough: 'stuff it' sounds like a rude dismissal but is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper cover holds letters, and filling such covers is classic temp work.

clue.text: PR operation one has following wetlands' appeal?

indicators.note: the first piece comes after the rest in the answer

parts.note: charm means appeal or attractiveness
the possessive reads as of fens, fens being wetlands
I have, shortened to I'VE

explanation.surface: A publicity drive promoting the attraction of marshy country.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fens are low-lying marshland in eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A public-relations campaign of flattery to win people over.

clue.text: Nice gal, groomed and pure

indicators.note: grooming rearranges hair, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A well-turned-out, virtuous young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Like an angel: innocent and virtuous.

clue.text: Hearing aids for the gullible

indicators.note: what one hears is the sound only, signalling a word that sounds like another

parts.note: succours are aids or help

explanation.surface: Hearing devices aimed at credulous people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing aids' looks like one phrase for deaf people, but 'Hearing' is the sound signal on 'aids'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gullible people are easily fooled dupes.

clue.text: Figure Italy's own goal valid

parts.note: I is the international vehicle code for Italy, plus S for the possessive
OG is the abbreviation for own goal in football
on means valid, as in 'the deal is on'

explanation.surface: Italy's football team counts an own goal as legitimate.
explanation.definitionFit: A geometric shape with all angles equal is this kind of figure.

clue.text: Second hand fairy stories may be put away here

definitions.text: stories may be put away here

parts.note: an elf is a fairy

explanation.surface: Second-hand fairy-tale books are stored away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second hand' and 'fairy stories' read as phrases but split into S, H, ELF and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Books, stories included, are stored on a ledge in a bookcase.

clue.text: School event at which lots of presents are expected?

definitions.text: School event at which lots of presents are expected?

parts.words: School event at which lots of presents are expected?
parts.note: pupils answer 'present' when their name is read out, not gifts

explanation.walkthrough: 'presents' suggests gifts; it is the reply 'Present!' at registration.
explanation.definitionFit: A reading of a register of names to check attendance.

clue.text: Full bin?

definitions.meaning: Bin is the first part of the name of Osama bin ..., so the name follows it

explanation.walkthrough: The rubbish bin is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavily loaded, and the surname that follows Osama bin.

clue.text: Around duck, do half the cooked nuts and pulses etc.

indicators.note: the shuffled letters go around the zero letter, holding it inside
cooked suggests the letters are fiddled into a new order

parts.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so O

explanation.surface: A recipe: around a duck, cook half the ingredients with nuts and pulses.
explanation.walkthrough: DO HALF THE shuffles to HEALTHFOD, with O added to make FOOD.
explanation.definitionFit: Wholesome natural produce such as nuts and pulses is sold in such shops.

clue.text: Show where post office used to be?

parts.note: ex- means former

explanation.surface: Someone points out a former post office site.
explanation.definitionFit: A large exhibition, short for exposition.

clue.text: Ineffectual result of censoring Father Ted?

definitions.text: Ineffectual result of censoring Father Ted?

parts.words: Ineffectual result of censoring Father Ted?
parts.note: the sitcom's favourite expletive cut out would leave the show without its feck, a state of being useless

explanation.walkthrough: Father Ted is an Irish TV sitcom whose Father Jack constantly shouts 'Feck!'.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means helplessness or lack of effectiveness.
